clue.text: Pretty fly driver, like tony weller

definitions.meaning: the Royal ... is a showy, brightly dressed fishing fly used by anglers
Tony Weller, father of Sam in Dickens's Pickwick Papers, drives a stagecoach for a living

explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a classic artificial trout fly and the driver of a horse-drawn coach, Tony Weller's trade in Pickwick.

clue.text: Village poet heard to grumble

indicators.note: heard tells us the word for grumbling is to be taken as it is spoken, not as written

parts.note: to crab is to complain or grumble peevishly

explanation.surface: A rustic versifier is overheard complaining.
explanation.walkthrough: George Crabbe wrote the long poem The Village (1783), so 'Village poet' is a fair definition by his best-known work.
explanation.definitionFit: George Crabbe, the Suffolk clergyman-poet, is known chiefly as author of the poem The Village.

clue.text: Hasten to reform city state

indicators.note: to reform is to form again, so the letters of the word before are reshaped

explanation.surface: An urgent call to remake a classical polity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to reform' rearranges HASTEN into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek polis centred on the Acropolis was a self-governing city state, the model of the type.

clue.text: Greene protagonist seen in a minor placing

definitions.text: Greene protagonist seen in a minor placing

parts.words: Greene protagonist seen in a minor placing
parts.note: the villain of Graham Greene's The Third Man, and third man is also a lowly fielding position in cricket, so a minor placing

explanation.walkthrough: Third man is a cricket fielding position behind the wicket on the off side; third is also a minor finishing place.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Greene's racketeer is the title figure of The Third Man, and third is a minor placing in any race.

clue.text: Source of Bunthorne's exquisite taste

parts.note: Reginald Bunthorne in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience is a fleshly poet who parodies the art-for-art's-sake movement of Wilde's day

explanation.definitionFit: Bunthorne's lilies and languor send up the late-Victorian cult of beauty for its own sake.

clue.text: They represent a start for Jewish men of letters

definitions.text: They represent a start for Jewish men of letters

parts.words: They represent a start for Jewish men of letters
parts.note: the first character of the Hebrew alphabet is where any Hebrew writer's alphabet begins

explanation.definitionFit: Each is the opening character of the Hebrew alphabet, the start of every Jewish scribe's set of letters.

clue.text: What all men are, as David hastily said

definitions.text: What all men are, as David hastily said

parts.words: What all men are, as David hastily said
parts.note: Psalm 116, attributed to David, says 'I said in my haste, All men are' false speakers

explanation.definitionFit: Psalm 116:11 in the King James Bible: 'I said in my haste, All men are' untruthful people.

clue.text: Spare one, in a way, from cast

indicators.note: in a way here means arranged after a fashion, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A theatre manager drops a spare actor from the company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a way' rearranges SPAREONE into the answer, as in dramatis personae, the list of characters.
explanation.definitionFit: Dramatis personae is the list of characters in a play, so the Latin plural stands for its cast.

clue.text: Streaked, like Hamlet's father's beard

definitions.meaning: marked with grey or white lines, as greying hair is
Horatio describes the Ghost's beard as 'A sable ...' in Hamlet, Act 1

explanation.definitionFit: Hair turning grey is streaked with white, and Horatio calls the Ghost's beard 'a sable silvered'.

clue.text: Bad mishap or wise remark?

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters are spoilt and must be put into a new order

explanation.surface: Asks whether a remark is a blunder or a piece of wisdom.
explanation.definitionFit: A pithy maxim expressing a general truth is a wise saying.

clue.text: "Oh roses for the flush of youth/ And — for the perfect prime" (C. G. Rossetti)

definitions.text: "Oh roses for the flush of youth/ And — for the perfect prime" (C. G. Rossetti)

parts.words: "Oh roses for the flush of youth/ And — for the perfect prime" (C. G. Rossetti)
parts.note: the missing word from Christina Rossetti's song is the evergreen leaf awarded for achievement in maturity

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue: the dash marks the word to supply from Christina Rossetti's 'Song' ('Oh roses for the flush of youth').
explanation.definitionFit: Rossetti's 'Song' pairs roses with youth and the bay leaf of victory with the prime of life.

clue.text: Dailies somehow retain scribbler

parts.note: dailies are daily newspapers

indicators.note: somehow says the letters of the next word come out in some order or other

explanation.surface: Newspapers employ a hack who keeps on writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges RETAIN to STAINER. A paper-stainer was originally a wallpaper maker, then a contemptuous name for a poor writer.
explanation.definitionFit: A paper-stainer is a dismissive old term for a hack who merely blots pages with ink.

clue.text: Hornung narrator seen at Playboy Club

definitions.meaning: ... Manders tells the Raffles stories of E. W. Hornung, as Watson tells Holmes's
the waitresses at Playboy Clubs wore rabbit ears and tails

explanation.definitionFit: Raffles's sidekick and chronicler shares his nickname with the costumed hostesses of Hefner's clubs.

clue.text: Memorial for Dickens's murderous Bradley

definitions.meaning: a stone set over a grave in memory of the dead
the schoolmaster in Our Mutual Friend who attacks Eugene Wrayburn

explanation.definitionFit: A grave marker serves as a memorial, and the jealous schoolmaster in Our Mutual Friend bears that surname.

clue.text: Respectable Windsor woman sees smart pig discomfited

indicators.note: discomfited means thrown into disorder, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A proper lady of Windsor is upset to see a clever pig.
explanation.walkthrough: 'discomfited' rearranges SEESSMARTPIG into the answer, one of Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Merry Wives of Windsor, Mrs Page is a virtuous wife who outwits Falstaff.

clue.text: "The real character of is beneath the surface, and beyond the powers of gush to disclose." (Robertson Davies)

definitions.text: "The real character of is beneath the surface, and beyond the powers of gush to disclose." (Robertson Davies)

parts.words: "The real character of is beneath the surface, and beyond the powers of gush to disclose." (Robertson Davies)
parts.note: the missing name is the fictional Ontario cathedral town of Robertson Davies's first trilogy of novels

explanation.walkthrough: A quotation clue with the place name left out after 'of'; Davies's three novels are known as the trilogy named after that town.
explanation.definitionFit: Robertson Davies set Tempest-Tost, Leaven of Malice and A Mixture of Frailties in an invented Canadian town of that name.

clue.text: Kant, for example, as saviour

definitions.meaning: Kant's first name, so he is an example of a man bearing it
the Hebrew name meaning 'God with us', given to the promised Messiah in Isaiah

explanation.definitionFit: The philosopher Kant bore this given name, which Isaiah's prophecy applies to the Messiah, Christ the Redeemer.

clue.text: Charming spelling of Merlin?

parts.note: not how to write the wizard's name but the enchanting spells he casts

explanation.definitionFit: Merlin's casting of spells and charms is magic art of the highest order.

clue.text: Dorset writer's Miss Rook, dug up in "Casterbridge" (66)

parts.note: a miss is an unmarried girl, a maiden
in chess the rook is also called the castle

explanation.surface: A spinster in Thomas Hardy's fiction, called Miss Rook, is exhumed in his Casterbridge.
explanation.walkthrough: Hardy, the Dorset writer, called Dorchester Casterbridge; the Iron Age hillfort just outside it was excavated by archaeologists, hence 'dug up'. The printed '(66)' is a garbled count.
explanation.definitionFit: The great Iron Age hillfort beside Dorchester was famously excavated by Mortimer Wheeler in the 1930s.

clue.text: Graduate gets Scandinavian backing for priestess

parts.note: an MA, Master of Arts, is a graduate

indicators.note: backing means going in reverse, so the Scandinavian word is read the other way

parts.note: a Dane is a Scandinavian from Denmark

explanation.surface: A university graduate wins the support of a Norse man in pursuit of a holy woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Maenads were frenzied female votaries of Dionysus, priestesses in his orgiastic rites.

clue.text: Story caption

definitions.meaning: a traditional tale handed down from the past
the words printed beneath a picture or on a map key

explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a traditional tale and the explanatory text under an illustration or on a map.

clue.text: Tsarevna in Anderson fairy tale?

parts.note: not Hans Andersen's stories but Anna Anderson's long-disproved claim to be the Tsar's surviving youngest daughter

explanation.definitionFit: Anna Anderson claimed for decades to be the Tsar's youngest daughter; DNA tests proved her claim a fiction.

clue.text: Uptight, and imperfect, possibly

definitions.meaning: the imperfect is one example of a grammatical verb form expressing time

explanation.definitionFit: The word means nervously strained, and in grammar the imperfect is one verb form of that kind.

clue.text: Delete English level

parts.note: rase is an old spelling of raze, to level a building to the ground

explanation.surface: An instruction to cut English to one standard.
explanation.walkthrough: RASE is an archaic spelling of raze, to flatten.
explanation.definitionFit: To expunge or wipe out text is to remove it entirely.

clue.text: Found inept, but full of spirit

indicators.note: full of says the words before it contain the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: Someone is judged incompetent, though still lively.
explanation.walkthrough: 'full of' finds the answer inside 'foUND INEpt'. 'Spirit' here is not liveliness but a water sprite of folklore.
explanation.definitionFit: An undine is an elemental water nymph in Paracelsus and in Fouqué's romance.

clue.text: Example of article on the church, after this month

indicators.note: after places the article and church after the abbreviation for this month

parts.note: inst., short for instant, means of the current month in old business letters
an is the indefinite article
CE stands for the Church of England

explanation.surface: A model of a piece written about the church, dated later this month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'inst.' (instant) is an old commercial abbreviation meaning 'of this month'.
explanation.definitionFit: A case or illustration offered as one of a kind is an example.

clue.text: Secular balladeers?

parts.note: people outside the clergy, punningly read as men who sing lays, old narrative songs

explanation.definitionFit: Non-clerical people are the opposite of priests, and a lay is a ballad, so they might be its singers.

clue.text: Tong manages to contain confused noise in island

indicators.note: to contain means the gang word holds the other piece within it

parts.note: a tong is a Chinese secret society, a triad

indicators.note: confused says the three letters of the noise word are turned about, here simply read back to front

parts.note: din is loud noise

explanation.surface: A Chinese gang struggles to suppress a racket on a Caribbean island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' jumbles the three-letter word for noise, which here just reverses it to NID; 'to contain' then wraps the gang word round it. A tong is a Chinese secret society.
explanation.definitionFit: The larger of the two islands of the Caribbean republic lies just off Venezuela.
